channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Foreword
item.description: Barry Humphries' foreword to 'Knockers', a mock-defensive survey of Australian knockery aimed at expatriates, critics and the film industry, recalling his own drubbing over an 'Aussie slang shocks Britain' headline and Dick Bentley's BBC Australia Day broadcast.

item.title: Knockers
item.description: Opens 'Knockers' by tracing the Australian compulsion to cut down its own achievers, from a Melbourne newspaper importing a London editor to soothe its colonial cringe, through visiting critics from James Cameron to Clement Freud, to the vicious reception of the Sydney Opera House and Australian writers at home.

item.title: Introduction
item.description: Opens 'No Brains on Tuesday' by recounting Keith Dunstan's 1985 defection from the Sun News-Pictorial, where his father had been General Manager, to write for the Age and Sydney Morning Herald, and the guilt, gracious phone calls and one cold shoulder that followed.

item.title: Who Smashes the Beethoven, Bach and Brahms LPs?
item.description: A column on the death of the vinyl LP as Polygram stops pressing new titles, tracing Keith Dunstan's own audio history from an HMV portable gramophone and 78s smashed with a hammer through to CD and the first Compact Disc Video players.

item.title: Your De-palatisation Guide
item.description: A tongue-in-cheek training program for wine lovers priced out of Grange Hermitage and Veuve Cliquot, working down through the grades to Coolibah cask at $7.99, extended to equivalent deprogramming courses for golfers, Bridge addicts, chocolate lovers and the incurable football fan.

item.title: There's Sex in Lolly Water
item.description: A survey of increasingly sexualised soft drink advertising, from Coca-Cola's frenzy and Tina Turner's writhing for Pepsi to spa water ads that promise everything, contrasted against the strict codes preventing beer advertisers from suggesting any pleasurable effect at all, with three proposed scenarios showing how soft drink ads could instead honestly reflect Australian life.

item.title: Dear Viewer
item.description: Episode four of the winemaking mini-series, in which toy poodle Lotte defeats the starlings, three tonnes of pinot noir are harvested, a power crusher replaces the virgins, and an electric blanket and hair dryer are requisitioned from the house for malolactic fermentation.

item.title: Loving Messages from the Chairman
item.description: An appreciative survey of the increasingly lavish company annual reports arriving in the letterbox, from the National Australia Bank's directors wandering elegantly down a marble staircase to the Lend Lease report's sapphire-blue portrait of Mr Dusseldorp and a ballerina held aloft by a site carpenter.

item.title: Would a Tax on the Waistline Help?
item.description: A detailed proposal for NICK, the New Inspired Consumption Kill, as a more rational alternative to the consumption tax, targeting automobiles for their emissions, graffiti pens, plastic bags, outdoor advertising, noisy motorbikes, television repeats, corporate take-over bids and the booming diet industry.

item.title: The Intelligent Man's Budget Guide
item.description: An A-to-Z economic dictionary for the bewildered citizen, defining Accord, Deficit, Gearing, J-curve, Pipeline and Zero in terms of actual Australian experience under Hawke, Keating and Kirner rather than Treasury optimism.

item.title: A Prostate Could Make You AA
item.description: The indignities of the modern credit-rating system, from Moody's down-grading the State Bank and a credit card application requiring a month-long inquisition, to an automatic teller swallowing a card and a South Yarra liquor store refusing a cheque, culminating in the observation that Bob Hawke's prostate operation will surely restore his public approval rating to Aaa.

item.title: Do Any of us Get Paid Enough?
item.description: A column on fair wages, arguing that a Flinders baker, Montsalvat violin and piano makers, leg spin bowlers, teachers, priests and policemen are chronically underpaid while golfers, share brokers, disc jockeys and newspaper columnists are a more interesting question altogether.

item.title: You Too Can Talk Like a Financial Wizard
item.description: A mock classroom seminar in financial journalism, in which students named Bondy, Elliott, Spalvins, Brierley, A'Court and Murdoch compete to find the most eloquent language for market crashes, corrections and recoveries, culminating in Murdoch attempting a take-over bid for the entire classroom.

item.title: Nearer to God in the Garden?
item.description: A pot obsession sparked by Tom Paterson's anonymous call to Kevin Heinze's ABC gardening program blaming him for a household of 6000 pots, matched by Keith Dunstan's own horror stories of orchid rotation plans, lavender drying and seaweed expeditions to the beach.

item.title: God Save Fish'n'Chips
item.description: A defence of fish and chips and Melbourne's under-rated shark meat, sold for decades as 'flake', against the American fast-food invasion, widening into a tally of other indigenous Melbourne treats, from meat pies to dim sims to hot crumpets, now under threat.

item.title: Rows and Rows of Roses
item.description: An account of catching the rose disease: 119 plants and still not enough, conversations conducted entirely to the roses rather than to each other, and the full cast of rose-named celebrities from Mrs Thatcher to Dolly Parton.

item.title: Oh for a Cottage Garden!
item.description: A survey of Australian garden fashions from all-native nationalism after Alan Bond won the America's Cup to the current English cottage garden craze, guided by nursery man Paul Hooper and featuring a $40,000 gazebo with Michelangelo's David lurking behind the delphiniums.

item.title: Spring is the Thunder of the Two Stroke
item.description: John Keats asked where the songs of spring had gone; the answer is that they have been drowned by two-stroke mowers, garden tractors with disc brakes and five-speed cruise control, power-rakes, whipper snippers and wood chippers that have turned the suburban garden into an engine room.

item.title: Battling the Berry
item.description: A lament over blackberries engulfing Keith Dunstan's farmlet, relief at the blackberry rust being tested at the Werribee research station, and a counter-proposal that Von Mueller's bust in the Botanic Gardens be joined by busts to the men who introduced mynas, sparrows, rabbits, foxes and cane toads.

item.title: Are Pitches Human?
item.description: A mock-scientific proposal for a summit chaired by Bob Hawke to design the perfect artificial cricket pitch, prompted by furious complaints that English curators are doctoring pitches against Australia's fast attack at Trent Bridge and Old Trafford.

item.title: Oh Freddie and Sir Leonard, Now it's the Foster's Oval
item.description: The naming of London's Kennington Oval after Foster's beer, with a wry tour through its history from Spofforth's 1882 Ashes triumph to Len Hutton's record score, via Keith Miller throwing a bottle at the dressing-room clock in 1953.

item.title: Couldn't the Cricketers Have Hats With Pretty Ribbons?
item.description: An argument against numbers on cricketers' backs in favour of returning to the 1862 convention of dove-coloured shirts with red spots and straw hats trimmed with magenta ribbon, with coloured ribbons on the arm to identify players and the dancing duck on the electronic scoreboard as the ultimate modern indignity.

item.title: Would You Kiss a Merv Hughes Moustache?
item.description: A meditation on the invasion of kissing in public life, from Brezhnev bear-hugging Kissinger and Jimmy Carter startling the Queen Mother, to Dennis Lillee starting the hugging fashion in cricket and the thought of kissing Merv Hughes's moustache or Alan Border's beard.

item.title: The Addiction of Cricket
item.description: A confession of cricket addiction: living 50 metres from a ground, the cry of 'OWZAT' as the most beautiful sound in nature, sleeping with an ear plug tuned to overseas Tests at 2.30 a.m., Ray Lindwall's psychological warm-up routine and Clarrie Grimmett as the supreme leg-spin artist.

item.title: The Pleasure of Thrashing the Poms
item.description: The deep tribal satisfaction of beating England at cricket, from Spofforth's 1882 Melbourne homecoming with gold medals and electric lights to Ted Dexter's frank admission in Wisden that Englishmen take an unreasonable dislike to Australians, with a belated plea for sportsmanship toward Graham Gooch's men.

item.title: Goodbye to the Daily at Dawn
item.description: A eulogy for the Sun News-Pictorial on its 1990 merger into the Herald Sun, recalling the Sun-Herald rivalry Keith Dunstan grew up inside as the son of the Sun's General Manager, and the newsroom rituals lost with it, from the DRUM of the presses to bylines that had to be earned.

item.title: The Glory of Grass
item.description: A lament for the disappearing grass tennis court, tracing its replacement by synthetic Plexipave at Melbourne's Jolimont stadium and the American invention of plastic grass, and arguing the LTAA should protect Australia's remaining grass courts before they vanish like the backyard courts subdivided after World War Two.

item.title: Let Us Spray
item.description: Keith Dunstan's account of accidentally spraying his entire Mornington Peninsula vineyard and his wife's rose garden with weedkiller instead of fungicide, and the frantic three-hour hosing operation with neighbours that saved all 1200 vines.

item.title: Getting the Bird
item.description: A battle-weary account of Mornington Peninsula vignerons' escalating war against birds devouring their grapes, from a Bob Hawke scarecrow and Frife shells to rocket warfare, scare guns and a neighbour's confession when asked which birds he had admired that month.

item.title: Getting the Bird (Part 2)
item.description: Advice pours in from around Australia on deterring vineyard birds, from fermenting-gruel hangovers to electrified bait traps and revolving mirror units, and the Easter vintage goes ahead with yellow plastic netting, panty hose over individual bunches, and granddaughters Hannah and Isabel recruited to foot-tramp the pinot noir.
